title: Supreme Court Says Two-Child Norm Has Lost Relevance as Fertility Falls, Sends 2003 Ruling to Larger Bench
excerpt: A bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe held that laws penalising more than two children rest on a fear of overpopulation that has crumbled as India fertility rate fell to 1.9, and referred the 2003 Javed judgment that upheld such disqualifications to a larger bench.
body:
• The Supreme Court on Wednesday said laws penalising people for having more than two children have lost their relevance, holding that the fear of overpopulation underpinning them has crumbled with demographic change.
  • India total fertility rate has fallen from 3.0 in 2003 to 1.9, below the 2.1 replacement level; the bench warned of an ageing population and a shrinking working-age share.
  • The bench did NOT strike down any law: it referred the 2003 Javed v State of Haryana judgment — which upheld two-child disqualifications for panchayat posts — to a larger bench for reconsideration.
  • In the case before it, the court set aside the disqualification of Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, a former Maharashtra sarpanch removed after her third child; several states, including Assam, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha and Uttarakhand, still retain two-child norms.

The Supreme Court has put India two-child laws on the path to reconsideration. A bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said on Wednesday that laws penalising having more than two children have lost their relevance, because the fear of overpopulation that justified them has crumbled in the face of demographic change, according to Live Law.

The demographic ground has moved

The numbers drove the reasoning. India total fertility rate has fallen from 3.0 in 2003 to 1.9, below the replacement level of 2.1, and the bench warned that the policy problem is inverting: an ageing population and a shrinking share of working-age people. The court also noted that China abandoned its one-child policy in 2015 and later moved to incentivise three children, yet its demographics did not reverse — evidence, in the bench treatment, that coercive limits and demographic outcomes are no longer connected the way they were assumed to be in 2003.

What the court did, and did not do

The bench referred Javed v State of Haryana, the 2003 three-judge judgment that upheld the Haryana Panchayati Raj Act disqualifications as not violating Article 14, to a larger bench. It did not strike down any statute, and two-child disqualifications remain in force until the larger bench decides. What the bench did say, in strong terms, is that such disqualification violates reproductive autonomy under Article 21 and forces an unconscionable choice between bearing children and democratic participation, Bar and Bench reported.

The case that carried the question

The appeal was brought by Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, a former sarpanch of Kakoda Gram Panchayat in Maharashtra, who was disqualified under Section 14(1)(j-1) of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959 — the two-child cap effective September 13, 2000 — after her third child. The Additional Collector, Buldhana disqualified her in October 2024, the Additional Commissioner, Amravati dismissed her appeal, and the Bombay High Court upheld the disqualification in August 2025 on the basis of the third child birth certificate. The Supreme Court set aside her disqualification.

The wider landscape, compiled by the amicus curiae Rukmini Bobde and noted by the court, is a patchwork: seven states have repealed the two-child norm and 15 never had such a policy, while states still retaining it include Assam, Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Odisha and Uttarakhand, according to Live Law. The larger bench hearing is now the event to watch: its decision will determine whether disqualification for a third child survives anywhere in India local government.
